explanations.explanation: Genesis 8:1 says, "And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside." Just a wind, no fireworks, and the water starts going down. The same verse says God remembered Noah and every animal with him in the ark. I would have guessed something louder, so it's a good thing I'm just the cookie stamper.

A pillar of fire sounds dramatic, but it isn't what the text says. Genesis 8:1 says, "And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside." Fire and a flood in one verse would be a very confusing day for everybody. The wind comes first, and then the waters begin to subside.

A swarm of locusts would be a lot of extra guests for a boat that's already full of animals. Genesis 8:1 says, "And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside." So what God sends is a wind, not a swarm. Easy to mix up when your mind is on a crowded boat, friend.

Not quite, friend. Genesis 8:3 says, "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." That's 150 days, not one. My oven takes a good while to cool off, and that's only one little oven.
False it is. Genesis 8:3 says the waters "receded steadily" and that after 150 days they had gone down. Steady, not sudden. I think anybody who has waited on a slow cooling rack knows the feeling.

Genesis 8:4 says the ark "came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." Notice it says mountains, plural. After all those months afloat, the boat finally has something solid under it. I bet the whole ark felt that landing.

Gilboa isn't in this story, friend. Genesis 8:4 says the ark "came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." Mountain names are easy to mix up. I mix up my own oven dials all the time, so no hard feelings.

Hills sound like a gentler landing, but Genesis 8:4 says the ark "came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." The text says mountains, not hills. Samaria doesn't show up in this passage at all. Ararat is the name to hold onto.

Mountains it is. Genesis 8:5 says, "on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible." Just the tops, so the rest is still under the water. I think that was a good day on the ark.

Trees would be a welcome sight, but this verse doesn't mention any. Genesis 8:5 says, "the tops of the mountains became visible." The next plant that shows up in this story is an olive leaf, and that's not until Genesis 8:11. For now, the mountaintops are what's peeking out.

No towers in this part of the story, friend. Genesis 8:5 says, "the tops of the mountains became visible." It's mountaintops in this verse, and nobody is hiring a construction crew. No towers, no trees, just mountaintops waving hello.

True. Genesis 8:7 says the raven "kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." Back and forth, back and forth, for a long stretch. That bird racked up some serious air miles.

That one is actually true. Genesis 8:7 says the raven "kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." So it was still at it long after Noah sent it out. I get tired just reading about it.

explanations.answer: She finds nowhere to land and returns
explanations.explanation: Genesis 8:9 says the dove "found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark." The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So she comes back with nothing, and Noah reaches out his hand to bring her inside. I think that was a long flight for a short answer.

explanations.answer: She stays out until the next morning
explanations.explanation: She didn't stay out, friend. Genesis 8:9 says she "found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark." The verse says nothing about her spending the night out there. I think that little bird was ready to be back inside.

explanations.answer: She builds a nest in a tree
explanations.explanation: Hard to build a nest when you can't even find a place to rest your foot. Genesis 8:9 says she found none, "because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth." So she returned to Noah in the ark. No nest on this trip.

Genesis 8:11 says the dove returned to him in the evening "with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." One leaf, and it tells Noah something big. The same verse says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." Small package, big news.

Fig leaves do show up in the Bible, back in Genesis 3:7, but not on this dove's flight. Genesis 8:11 says she came back with "a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." Different leaf, different story. It's an olive leaf this time, friend.
A whole palm branch would be a lot for one little beak. Genesis 8:11 says the dove returned "with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." Just one leaf. No branch required.
Receded is the word. Genesis 8:11 says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." Noah didn't need a weather report. All he needed was one freshly plucked leaf.

Risen would be the opposite direction, friend. Genesis 8:11 says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." The waters are going down, not up. A leaf coming back with the dove is good news.

Stilled sounds peaceful, but it isn't the word in the verse. Genesis 8:11 says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." Receded means the water pulled back and went down, not just that it got quiet. Noah learned that from a leaf.

Not this time. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him." Three trips, and the third one had no return flight. The second trip is the one where she comes back.

False it is. Genesis 8:12 says Noah waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, "but this time she did not return to him." I think I'd be checking the sky every five minutes. Noah had already waited a lot of days by then.

Dry it is. Genesis 8:13 says Noah "removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry." Then Genesis 8:14 says that by the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry. Surface dry first, then all the way dry.

Flooded is how the world looked for a long time, but not at this moment. Genesis 8:13 says the waters had dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering and "saw that the surface of the ground was dry." That's a big change from the start of this passage.
Frozen doesn't show up anywhere in this scene, friend. Genesis 8:13 says Noah "saw that the surface of the ground was dry." No ice and no snow, just dry ground. Noah finally gets a good look at it.

Leave is the word. Genesis 8:16 says God tells Noah, "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." Then Genesis 8:18 says, "So Noah came out." The one who tells him it's time is God.
Nobody hands Noah a toolbox here. Genesis 8:16 has God say, "Come out of the ark." It's time to leave, not time to fix anything. The ark's job is done.

Sealing belongs to the other end of the story. Back in Genesis 6:14, the ark gets coated with pitch inside and out. Here in Genesis 8:16, God says, "Come out of the ark." So it's the opposite job, friend. Out, not in.

explanations.answer: So they can spread out and multiply
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. Genesis 8:17 says to bring them out "so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." A boat is a fine place to stay for a while. A whole earth is where they get to spread out.

explanations.answer: So Noah can count every one
explanations.explanation: God doesn't mention counting, friend. Genesis 8:17 gives the reason: "so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." Counting that crowd would take a while anyway. The point is the spreading and multiplying.

explanations.answer: So the ark can be taken apart
explanations.explanation: The ark never gets taken apart in this passage. Genesis 8:17 says to bring them out "so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." The reason is about the animals and the earth, not about the boat. That's the reason to hold onto.

Genesis 8:20 says Noah, "taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar." Clean animals and clean birds, every kind. The altar is the first thing the text has Noah build after stepping off the ark. I think he skipped unpacking.
Wild sounds exciting, but that's not the category. Genesis 8:20 says Noah took "from every kind of clean animal and clean bird." The word that sets the line is clean. Nothing in the verse says wild.
Age doesn't come up in this verse, friend. Genesis 8:20 says Noah took "from every kind of clean animal and clean bird." The word is clean, not young. That's the detail to hold onto.
True. Genesis 8:21 says the LORD "said in His heart, 'Never again will I curse the ground because of man.'" That's a promise. It comes right after the pleasing aroma of Noah's offering.
That one is actually true, friend. Genesis 8:21 says the LORD "said in His heart, 'Never again will I curse the ground because of man.'" Never again. The text puts it plainly.

explanations.answer: It is evil from his youth
explanations.explanation: Genesis 8:21 says "every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." Notice the promise comes right alongside it. The LORD says it "even though" that's true. A hard line, said plainly.

explanations.answer: It is pure from his youth
explanations.explanation: Pure would be lovely, but that's not what the verse says. Genesis 8:21 says "every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." The text is blunt about it. And the promise still comes, "even though" that's so.

explanations.answer: It is humble from his youth
explanations.explanation: I'd love to say humble. I'm still working on mine, and my hat is very tall. Genesis 8:21 says "every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." That's the word the text uses, friend.

That's not what He said, friend. Genesis 8:21 says, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." It's never again, not someday. Genesis 9:11 repeats it: "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."

False it is. Genesis 8:21 says, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." The word is never again. Genesis 9:11 says it again: "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."

True. Genesis 9:3 says everything that lives and moves will be food for them. Then Genesis 9:4 adds the limit: "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." I only handle cookies, so my kitchen rule is simpler: don't burn them.
That one is actually true, friend. Genesis 9:4 says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." Verse 3 allowed a lot, and verse 4 adds a limit. That's the catch.

explanations.answer: God made mankind in His own image
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. Genesis 9:6 says, "for in His own image God has made mankind." The weight of the verse is on who people are, not how many there are. Human life is serious because of that image.

explanations.answer: Few people are left after the flood
explanations.explanation: That sounds logical, but the verse doesn't give that reason. Genesis 9:6 says, "for in His own image God has made mankind." The reason is the image, not the headcount. God's reason doesn't depend on numbers.

explanations.answer: Men must answer to their rulers
explanations.explanation: Rulers don't show up in this verse, friend. In Genesis 9:5, God says, "I will demand an accounting from anyone who takes the life of his fellow man." The reason comes in Genesis 9:6: "for in His own image God has made mankind." The image is the reason.

Not quite, friend. Genesis 9:10 says the covenant is "with every living creature that was with you." That means the birds, the livestock and every beast of the earth too. The animals are included, not just the humans.

False it is. Genesis 9:10 says the covenant is with the birds, the livestock and every beast of the earth. It also says "every living thing that came out of the ark." Nobody who came off that boat is left out.

Genesis 9:11 says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth." Notice it's said two ways in the same verse. The promise names the waters of a flood.

Famine isn't what the covenant names, friend. Genesis 9:11 says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood." The covenant is stated in terms of a flood. That's the word to hold onto.
Fire isn't in this verse. Genesis 9:11 says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood." The covenant names one thing, the waters of a flood. Water, not fire.

Genesis 9:13 says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." The sign is the rainbow. My favorite color is the rainbow, so I may be biased. I can't pick just one color, friend.

Stars are a big deal in my bakery, since every finished cookie box lights my sky with one. But Genesis 9:13 says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds." The sign is a rainbow, not a star. Different sky, different sign.

A pillar of cloud shows up later in the Bible, in Exodus 13:21, but not here. Genesis 9:13 says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds." Here the clouds are the stage and the rainbow is the show. That's the sign of this covenant.

Genesis 9:15 says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." The rainbow is the sign of that covenant. Verse 16 says He will see it and remember. That's the promise connected to the sign.

Gathering isn't in this verse, friend. Genesis 9:15 says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." The rainbow points back to the covenant. Remembering is the word.

Harvest does come up in this passage, in Genesis 8:22, along with seedtime, cold, heat, summer and winter. But the rainbow verse says something else. Genesis 9:15 says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." It's remembering the covenant.

Everlasting is the word. Genesis 9:16 says, "I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." Genesis 9:12 also calls it "a covenant for all generations to come." Not a word about it running out.

Conditional would mean it hangs on an if, but the verse doesn't say that. Genesis 9:16 calls it "the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." Genesis 9:12 says it's "a covenant for all generations to come." Everlasting is the word.

Seasons are in this passage, friend. Genesis 8:22 mentions summer and winter. But the covenant isn't seasonal. Genesis 9:16 calls it "the everlasting covenant," and Genesis 9:12 says it's "a covenant for all generations to come."
